questions.stem: Jake Morrison, 78, has come to a Williamstown GP with more than a month of yellow eyes. His wife has been giving him carrot juice, and he asks, "Is it the carrot juice?" His palms look faintly yellow. Which examination step best tells carotenaemia apart from true jaundice?
options: Inspect the palms and soles for yellow discolouration in daylight, comparing both sides
Inspect the sclera in natural light with the lower lid gently pulled down
Press on the nail bed and watch the colour as it blanches and refills over several seconds
Look for yellow discolouration of the nasolabial folds and forehead under room light
questions.why: Carotene builds up in the outer layer of the skin but spares the sclera. Bilirubin binds to the elastin of the sclera, so scleral icterus seen in natural light means true hyperbilirubinaemia rather than carotenaemia.
notes: Palms and soles turn yellow in both carotenaemia and jaundice, so yellow palms cannot separate the two.
Capillary refill tests peripheral perfusion and tells you nothing about what is causing the yellow colour.
Carotene tends to collect in the nasolabial folds and forehead, but jaundice also yellows the skin, so this sign does not separate them.

questions.stem: Jake, 78, has obstructive jaundice. His pancreatic-protocol CT shows a 32 mm hypoattenuating pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign, no vascular involvement and no metastases. The hepatobiliary MDT wants a tissue diagnosis. Which is the preferred way to get it?
options: Percutaneous CT-guided core biopsy of the pancreatic head mass
ERCP with brush cytology of the distal common bile duct
Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle biopsy of the mass
Diagnostic laparoscopy with biopsy of the pancreatic head
questions.why: EUS-guided fine-needle biopsy is the preferred way to get tissue from a pancreatic mass. It gives a high diagnostic yield, adds local staging, and avoids seeding tumour along a percutaneous tract in disease that may be resectable.
notes: A percutaneous biopsy risks seeding tumour along the needle tract and peritoneum in potentially curable disease, so it is kept for unresectable cases where EUS is not possible.
Brush cytology at ERCP has low sensitivity for pancreatic cancer. ERCP is used mainly for biliary drainage, not for diagnosis.
Laparoscopy is invasive and is used selectively for staging, to look for occult peritoneal disease, not as the first-line way to get tissue.

questions.stem: Jake, 78, has a pancreatic head mass blocking his common bile duct. Bilirubin is 186 µmol/L (mostly conjugated), ALP is 612 U/L, albumin is 32 g/L and INR is 1.4. He takes no anticoagulant. What is the most likely mechanism of his raised INR?
options: Bile salts cannot reach the gut to form micelles, so vitamin K is poorly absorbed
Hepatic synthesis of clotting factors has failed from established hepatic cirrhosis
Clotting factors are being consumed by tumour-driven chronic intravascular coagulation
Conjugated bilirubin directly inhibits gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors in liver
questions.why: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and needs bile salt micelles to be absorbed. Biliary obstruction therefore depletes factors II, VII, IX and X. This corrects with parenteral phytomenadione, which matters before EUS, ERCP or surgery.
notes: Nothing suggests cirrhosis (no stigmata, mildly low albumin, a cholestatic pattern). An INR that corrects with parenteral vitamin K points to malabsorption, not synthetic failure.
Nothing points to DIC: he is well and afebrile, and there is no thrombocytopenia or bleeding. DIC would also not explain an isolated mild INR rise.
Bilirubin does not inhibit the vitamin K-dependent carboxylase. The defect is a lack of vitamin K itself.

questions.stem: Jake's CT shows a pancreatic head mass with abrupt cut-off of both a dilated common bile duct (14 mm) and a dilated main pancreatic duct (6 mm): the double duct sign. Where do these two ducts normally join and drain, explaining why one head mass blocks both?
options: First (superior) part of the duodenum, beside the gastroduodenal artery
Third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, passing beneath the SMA
Duodenojejunal flexure, at the suspensory ligament of the duodenum
Second (descending) part of the duodenum, at the major duodenal papilla
questions.why: The distal common bile duct runs behind or through the pancreatic head and joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, so a head mass can block both ducts at once.
notes: The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, but the ducts do not drain there.
The third part of the duodenum crosses beneath the SMA (where SMA syndrome happens); no ducts drain into it.
The duodenojejunal flexure is where the duodenum meets the jejunum, well away from where the ducts drain.
